The author of the 'Harry Potter' series is J.K. Rowling.

The space station, known as the Aethelgard Outpost, orbited the desolate planet of Xylos, a world stripped of atmosphere and life by a cataclysmic solar flare three centuries prior. The station’s metallic corridors, constructed from recycled hull plating of early colonization ships, echoed with the solitary hum of machinery—a sound that had become the only constant in the lives of the few hundred residents who remained. These corridors were narrow and utilitarian, lined with flickering fluorescent lights that cast long, jagged shadows against the cold steel walls, emphasizing the isolation of the outpost.

Outside the reinforced viewing ports, a ballet of asteroids danced against the inky backdrop of space, their surfaces pitted and scarred by eons of cosmic radiation. These celestial bodies, remnants of a shattered moon, moved in slow, gravitational waltzes, occasionally colliding in silent, explosive bursts that sent debris spiraling into the void. The station’s sensors tracked these movements with relentless precision, for the debris field was not merely a spectacle but a hazard, threatening the fragile infrastructure that kept the outpost alive. The residents, bound by duty and necessity, watched this cosmic dance with a mix of awe and trepidation, knowing that their survival depended on the delicate balance between the station’s aging systems and the unforgiving nature of the void.
